title: Understanding Contract Basics
text:
A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. For it to be enforceable, the parties must have the capacity to enter into it, there must be a clear offer and acceptance, and each party must provide something of value, known as consideration. Courts generally expect the terms to be written in plain language so that both sides understand their obligations. Without these elements, a document may be considered void or voidable.

Many contracts also include a clause that limits liability, which restricts the amount one party may have to pay if something goes wrong. Another common provision is an indemnity clause, under which one party agrees to compensate the other for certain losses. Before signing, a careful reader should check how disputes will be resolved, since some agreements require arbitration instead of litigation. Ignoring these details can lead to unexpected costs.

questions.text: According to the passage, what is consideration?
options: Something of value that each party provides
A written copy of the terms
A formal decision made by a judge
An official signature on the document

questions.text: What does an indemnity clause require?
options: Both parties to share profits equally
The parties to resolve disputes in court
One party to compensate the other for certain losses
The contract to be written in plain language

questions.text: Why would a careful reader check how disputes will be resolved before signing?
options: Because disputes always end up in court
Because the chosen method may affect how and where conflicts are handled
Because it changes the parties' legal capacity
Because arbitration is illegal in most countries

questions.text: What can be inferred about a contract that lacks the required elements?
options: It becomes more valuable to both parties
It must be rewritten by a judge automatically
It is always enforceable if signed in public
It may be considered void or voidable

vocabulary.definition: legal responsibility for a loss or harm
a method of settling disputes outside a court
a promise to compensate someone for a loss

paragraph_translations: Un contrato es un acuerdo jurídicamente vinculante entre dos o más partes. Para que sea exigible, las partes deben tener capacidad para celebrarlo, debe haber una oferta clara y una aceptación, y cada parte debe aportar algo de valor, conocido como contraprestación. Los tribunales suelen esperar que los términos estén redactados en un lenguaje sencillo para que ambas partes comprendan sus obligaciones. Sin estos elementos, un documento puede considerarse nulo o anulable.

Muchos contratos también incluyen una cláusula que limita la responsabilidad, que restringe la cantidad que una parte puede tener que pagar si algo sale mal. Otra disposición común es la cláusula de indemnidad, en virtud de la cual una parte acepta compensar a la otra por ciertas pérdidas. Antes de firmar, un lector atento debe revisar cómo se resolverán las disputas, ya que algunos acuerdos exigen arbitraje en lugar de litigio. Ignorar estos detalles puede generar costes inesperados.
